<document>
<title>The World's Billionaires</title>
<fragment>
In the 37th annual *Forbes* list of the world's billionaires, the list included 2,640 billionaires with a total net wealth of $12.2 trillion, down 28 members and $500 billion from 2022. Over half of the list is less wealthy compared to the previous year, including Elon Musk, who fell from No. 1 to No. 2.[2] The list also marks for the first time a French citizen was in the top position as well as a non-American for the first time since 2013 when the Mexican Carlos Slim Helu was the world's richest person. The list, like in 2022, counted 15 under 30 billionaires with the richest of them being Red Bull heir Mark Mateschitz with a net worth of $34.7 billion. The youngest of the lot were Clemente Del Vecchio, heir to the Luxottica fortune shared with his six siblings and stepmother, and Kim Jung-yang, whose fortune lies in Japanese-South Korean gaming giant Nexon, both under-20s.[10]






</fragment>
<fragment>
In the 32nd annual *Forbes* list of the world's billionaires, the aggregate wealth of the top 20 richest people on Earth amounted to about 13 percent of all billionaires' fortunes combined.[15] A record of 2,208 billionaires were in the ranking and the total wealth was $9.1 trillion, up 18% since 2017. For the first time, Jeff Bezos was listed as the top billionaire due to Amazon's rising stock price that resulted in one person's biggest one-year gain in wealth ($35 billion) since *Forbes* started tracking in 1987.[15] The U.S. had the most billionaires in the world, with 585, while China was catching up with 476 when including Hong Kong, Macau and Taiwan; it had 372 when excluding those three places.[15] Forbes excluded Al-Walid bin Talal and all other Saudi billionaires due to the absence of accurate wealth estimations as a result of the 2017–19 Saudi Arabian purge.[16]






</fragment>
<fragment>
Since stock prices fluctuate rapidly, an individual's true wealth and ranking at the time of publication may vary from their situation when the list was compiled.[7]


When a living individual has dispersed his or her wealth to immediate family members it is included under a single listing (as a single "family fortune") provided that individual (the grantor) is still living. However, if a deceased billionaire's fortune has been dispersed, it will not appear as a single listing, and each recipient will only appear if his or her own total net worth is over a $Billion (his or her net worth will not be combined with family members')[7] Royal families and dictators that have their wealth contingent on a position are always excluded from these lists.[9]



## Annual rankings

[edit]


The rankings are published annually in March, so the net worths listed are snapshots taken at that time. These lists only show the top 10 wealthiest billionaires for each year.

The ***Forbes* 400** or **400 Richest Americans** is a list published by *Forbes* magazine of the wealthiest 400 American citizens who own assets in the U.S., ranked by net worth. The 400 was started by Malcolm Forbes in 1982 and the list is published annually around September.[2] Peter W. Bernstein and Annalyn Swan describe the *Forbes* 400 as capturing "a period of extraordinary individual and entrepreneurial energy, a time unlike the extended postwar years, from 1945 to 1982, when American society emphasized the power of corporations." Bernstein and Swan also describe it as representing "a powerful argument – and sometimes a dream – about the social value of wealth in contemporary America."[3]


Since 2014, *Forbes* has published a "self-made score" alongside the list, indicating the degree to which each *Forbes* 400 member is responsible for their own wealth.[4]

The *Forbes* 400 is a report of who has the most wealth in the United States. They annually create a list of the richest people in America to exhibit the shape of the economy. The magazine displays the story of someone's rise to fame, their company, age, industrial residence, and education. The list portrays the financial shift of trends, leadership positions, and growing philanthropy intentions.[5][6]



### First list (1982)

[edit]

In the first *Forbes* 400 list,[7] there were only 13 billionaires, and a net worth of US$75 million secured a spot on the list. The 1982 list represented 2.8% of the Gross Domestic Product of the United States. The 1982 *Forbes* 400 had 22.8% of the list composed of oil fortunes, with 15.3% from manufacturing, 9% from finance and only 3% from technology-driven fortunes. The state of New York had the most representation on the list with 77 members, followed by California with 48.[8]

<document>
<title>Forbes 400</title>
<fragment>

![](image)Billionaire wealth
The ***Forbes* 400** or **400 Richest Americans** is a list published by *Forbes* magazine of the wealthiest 400 American citizens who own assets in the U.S., ranked by net worth. The 400 was started by Malcolm Forbes in 1982 and the list is published annually around September.[2] Peter W. Bernstein and Annalyn Swan describe the *Forbes* 400 as capturing "a period of extraordinary individual and entrepreneurial energy, a time unlike the extended postwar years, from 1945 to 1982, when American society emphasized the power of corporations." Bernstein and Swan also describe it as representing "a powerful argument – and sometimes a dream – about the social value of wealth in contemporary America."[3]


Since 2014, *Forbes* has published a "self-made score" alongside the list, indicating the degree to which each *Forbes* 400 member is responsible for their own wealth.[4]

Over the first 25 years of the *Forbes* 400 list, 1,302 distinct people made the list. In that time period, 97 immigrants (7.5%) and 202 women (15.5%) made the list. Four of the top five richest people in the United States in 2006 were college dropouts: Bill Gates, Sheldon Adelson, Larry Ellison, and Paul Allen.[3]


A few articles draw on the *Forbes* 400 to test an evolutionary hypothesis called the Trivers–Willard hypothesis. This hypothesis predicts that parents of high socioeconomic status produce more male offspring than parents of lower socioeconomic status.[14] Whereas a 2009 study using data on the *Forbes* 400 shows a strong effect for U.S. billionaires that is consistent with the Trivers–Willard hypothesis,[15] a 2013 study shows some caveats: First, the result is only consistent for male, but not female, billionaires. Second, it can only be found among heirs and not self-made billionaires.[16]

Each year, *Forbes* employs a team of over 50 reporters from a variety of countries to track the activity of the world's wealthiest individuals[7] and sometimes groups or families – who share wealth. Preliminary surveys are sent to those who may qualify for the list. According to *Forbes*, they received three types of responses – some people try to inflate their wealth, others cooperate but leave out details, and some refuse to answer any questions.[8] Business deals are then scrutinized and estimates of valuable assets – land, homes, vehicles, artwork, etc. – are made. Interviews are conducted to vet the figures and improve the estimate of an individual's holdings. Finally, positions in a publicly traded stock are priced to market on a date roughly a month before publication. Privately held companies are priced by the prevailing price-to-sales or price-to-earnings ratios. Known debt is subtracted from assets to get a final estimate of an individual's estimated worth in United States dollars.

The ***Bloomberg Billionaires Index***, launched in March 2012, is a daily ranking of the world's 500 richest people based on their net worth.[3][4][5] It features a profile of each billionaire, and includes a tool that allows users to compare the fortunes of multiple billionaires. The index is updated every day at the close of trading in New York.[6]




## 2023 rankings

[edit]

The rankings are updated only on every trading day after the closing bell of every trading day based on New York's time.

Journalists have noted that the detailed methodology used for the index is more transparent than the "somewhat vaguer" calculation behind other lists.[19] "The Bloomberg listers say their estimates may be more accurate than the competition's because they have better data and reporting (from Bloomberg terminals and its reporting staff)."[20]



## Data visualization

[edit]

The full index is available online on the Bloomberg Terminal for free.[21] There are tools to compare the fortunes of multiple billionaires, track the billionaires whose assets change the most, and analyze the one-year performance of individual billionaires or billionaires grouped by industry, region or nation.[22][23]


Each billionaire's profile includes explanations of asset valuations and more details about each fortune.[8]

<document>
<title>Jeff Bezos</title>
<fragment>

Bezos attended the Student Science Training Program at the University of Florida. He was high school valedictorian, a National Merit Scholar,[33][34] and a Silver Knight Award winner in 1982.[33] In his graduation speech, Bezos told the audience he dreamed of the day when mankind would colonize space. A local newspaper quoted his intention "to get all people off the earth and see it turned into a huge national park".[35]


After graduating from high school in 1982, Bezos attended Princeton University. He initially majored in physics but later switched to electrical engineering and computer science.[36] Bezos was a member of the Quadrangle Club, one of Princeton's 11 eating clubs.[37] In addition, he was the president of the Princeton chapter of the Students for the Exploration and Development of Space (SEDS).[38][39] He had a 4.2 GPA and was elected to Phi Beta Kappa and Tau Beta Pi. Bezos graduated from Princeton in 1986 with a Bachelor of Science in Engineering (BSE), *summa cum laude*.[40]




</fragment>

Harvard students Cameron Winklevoss, Tyler Winklevoss, and Divya Narendra accused Zuckerberg of intentionally making them believe he would help them build a social network called HarvardConnection.com (later called ConnectU).[80] They filed a lawsuit in 2004; it was dismissed on a technicality on March 28, 2007. It was refiled soon thereafter in a federal court in Boston. Facebook countersued in regards to Social Butterfly, a project put out by The Winklevoss Chang Group, an alleged partnership between ConnectU and i2hub. On June 25, 2008, the case settled and Facebook agreed to transfer over 1.2 million common shares and pay $20 million in cash.[81]


In November 2007, confidential court documents were posted on the website of *02138*, a magazine that catered to Harvard alumni. They included Zuckerberg's Social Security number, his parents' home address, and his girlfriend's address. Though Facebook filed to have the documents removed, the judge ruled in favor of *02138*.[82]

Zuckerberg began using computers and writing software in middle school. In high school, he built a program that allowed all the computers between his house and his father's dental office to communicate with each other.[19][20] During Zuckerberg's high-school years, he worked to build a music player called the Synapse Media Player. The device used machine learning to learn the user's listening habits, which was posted to *Slashdot*[21] and received a rating of 3 out of 5 from *PC Magazine*.[22] A *New Yorker* profile said of Zuckerberg: "some kids played computer games. Mark created them."[14]



#### College years

[edit]


</fragment>
<fragment>
The *New Yorker* noted that by the time Zuckerberg began classes at Harvard in 2002, he had already achieved a "reputation as a programming prodigy". He studied psychology and computer science and belonged to Alpha Epsilon Pi and Kirkland House.[23][14][24] In his sophomore year, he wrote a program that he called CourseMatch, which allowed users to make class selection decisions based on the choices of other students and help them form study groups. Later, he created a different program he initially called Facemash that let students select the best-looking person from a choice of photos. Arie Hasit, Zuckerberg's roommate at the time, explained:




> We had books called Face Books, which included the names and pictures of everyone who lived in the student dorms. Zuckerberg took the company public in May 2012 with majority shares. In 2007, at age 23, he became the world's youngest self-made billionaire. **Steven Anthony Ballmer** (/ˈbɔːlmər/; March 24, 1956)[1] is an American billionaire businessman and investor who served as the chief executive officer of Microsoft from 2000 to 2014.[1] He is the owner of the Los Angeles Clippers of the National Basketball Association (NBA). He is a co-founder of Ballmer Group, a philanthropic investment company.[2] As of November 2023, *Bloomberg Billionaires Index* estimates his personal wealth at around $122 billion, making him the fifth-richest person in the world.[3]

In 1973, he attended college prep and engineering classes at Lawrence Technological University. He graduated as valedictorian from Detroit Country Day School, a private college preparatory school in Beverly Hills, Michigan, with a score of 790 on the mathematical section of the SAT[15][16] and was a National Merit Scholar.[17] (He eventually became a member of the school's board of directors.)


Ballmer, the first in his family to graduate college[18] ,attended Harvard University, where he was a manager for the Harvard Crimson football team and a member of the Fox Club, worked on *The Harvard Crimson* newspaper as well as the *Harvard Advocate*, and lived down the hall from fellow sophomore Bill Gates. He scored highly in the William Lowell Putnam Mathematical Competition, an exam sponsored by the Mathematical Association of America, scoring higher than Bill Gates.[19] He graduated *magna cum laude* with a Bachelor of Arts in applied mathematics and economics in 1977.[20][21]

<fragment>
Over the first 25 years of the *Forbes* 400 list, 1,302 distinct people made the list. In that time period, 97 immigrants (7.5%) and 202 women (15.5%) made the list. Four of the top five richest people in the United States in 2006 were college dropouts: Bill Gates, Sheldon Adelson, Larry Ellison, and Paul Allen.[3]


A few articles draw on the *Forbes* 400 to test an evolutionary hypothesis called the Trivers–Willard hypothesis. This hypothesis predicts that parents of high socioeconomic status produce more male offspring than parents of lower socioeconomic status.[14] Whereas a 2009 study using data on the *Forbes* 400 shows a strong effect for U.S. billionaires that is consistent with the Trivers–Willard hypothesis,[15] a 2013 study shows some caveats: First, the result is only consistent for male, but not female, billionaires. Second, it can only be found among heirs and not self-made billionaires.[16]


</fragment>
<fragment>

![](image)Billionaire wealth
The ***Forbes* 400** or **400 Richest Americans** is a list published by *Forbes* magazine of the wealthiest 400 American citizens who own assets in the U.S., ranked by net worth. The 400 was started by Malcolm Forbes in 1982 and the list is published annually around September.[2] Peter W. Bernstein and Annalyn Swan describe the *Forbes* 400 as capturing "a period of extraordinary individual and entrepreneurial energy, a time unlike the extended postwar years, from 1945 to 1982, when American society emphasized the power of corporations." Bernstein and Swan also describe it as representing "a powerful argument – and sometimes a dream – about the social value of wealth in contemporary America."[3]


Since 2014, *Forbes* has published a "self-made score" alongside the list, indicating the degree to which each *Forbes* 400 member is responsible for their own wealth.[4]

<title>Steve Ballmer</title>
<fragment>

In 1973, he attended college prep and engineering classes at Lawrence Technological University. **Steven Anthony Ballmer** (/ˈbɔːlmər/; March 24, 1956)[1] is an American billionaire businessman and investor who served as the chief executive officer of Microsoft from 2000 to 2014.[1] He is the owner of the Los Angeles Clippers of the National Basketball Association (NBA). He is a co-founder of Ballmer Group, a philanthropic investment company.[2] As of November 2023, *Bloomberg Billionaires Index* estimates his personal wealth at around $122 billion, making him the fifth-richest person in the world.[3]

Ballmer serves on the World Chairman's Council of the Jewish National Fund, which means he has donated US$1 million or more to the JNF.[104]



## USAFacts

[edit]

Ballmer launched USAFacts.org in 2017, a not-for-profit organization whose goal is to allow people to understand U.S. government revenue, spending and societal impact. He is reported to have contributed $10 million to fund teams of researchers who populated the website's database with official data.[105][106][107]



## Personal life

[edit]

In 1990, Ballmer married Connie Snyder;[108] they have three sons.[109]


The Ballmers live in Hunts Point, Washington.[110]

<title>Forbes 400</title>
<fragment>

![](image)Billionaire wealth
The ***Forbes* 400** or **400 Richest Americans** is a list published by *Forbes* magazine of the wealthiest 400 American citizens who own assets in the U.S., ranked by net worth. The 400 was started by Malcolm Forbes in 1982 and the list is published annually around September.[2] Peter W. Bernstein and Annalyn Swan describe the *Forbes* 400 as capturing "a period of extraordinary individual and entrepreneurial energy, a time unlike the extended postwar years, from 1945 to 1982, when American society emphasized the power of corporations." Bernstein and Swan also describe it as representing "a powerful argument – and sometimes a dream – about the social value of wealth in contemporary America."[3]


Since 2014, *Forbes* has published a "self-made score" alongside the list, indicating the degree to which each *Forbes* 400 member is responsible for their own wealth.[4]

[edit]

</fragment>
<fragment>
Over the first 25 years of the *Forbes* 400 list, 1,302 distinct people made the list. In that time period, 97 immigrants (7.5%) and 202 women (15.5%) made the list. Four of the top five richest people in the United States in 2006 were college dropouts: Bill Gates, Sheldon Adelson, Larry Ellison, and Paul Allen.[3]


A few articles draw on the *Forbes* 400 to test an evolutionary hypothesis called the Trivers–Willard hypothesis. This hypothesis predicts that parents of high socioeconomic status produce more male offspring than parents of lower socioeconomic status.[14] Whereas a 2009 study using data on the *Forbes* 400 shows a strong effect for U.S. billionaires that is consistent with the Trivers–Willard hypothesis,[15] a 2013 study shows some caveats: First, the result is only consistent for male, but not female, billionaires. Second, it can only be found among heirs and not self-made billionaires.[16]


</fragment>

<document>
<title>Sergey Brin</title>
<fragment>

Brin emigrated to the United States from the Soviet Union at the age of six. He earned his bachelor's degree at the University of Maryland, College Park, following in his father's and grandfather's footsteps by studying mathematics as well as computer science. After graduation, he enrolled in Stanford University to acquire a PhD in computer science. There he met Page, with whom he built a web search engine. The program became popular at Stanford, and they suspended their PhD studies to start up Google in Susan Wojcicki's garage in Menlo Park.[3]




## Early life and education

[edit]

Brin was born on August 21, 1973, in Moscow in the Soviet Union,[4] to Russian Jewish parents,[5] Mikhail and Eugenia Brin, both graduates of Moscow State University (MSU).[6] His father is a retired mathematics professor at the University of Maryland, and his mother is a researcher at NASA's Goddard Space Flight Center.[7][8]


</fragment>
<fragment>

Brin began his graduate study in computer science at Stanford University on a graduate fellowship from the National Science Foundation, receiving an M.S. in computer science in 1995.[11] As of 2008[update], he was on leave from his PhD studies at Stanford.[12]



## Search engine development

[edit]

![](image)Left to right, Eric Schmidt, Sergey Brin and Larry Page, 2008
During an orientation for new students at Stanford, he met Larry Page. The two men seemed to disagree on most subjects, but after spending time together they "became intellectual soul-mates and close friends." Brin's focus was on developing data mining systems while Page's was on extending "the concept of inferring the importance of a research paper from its citations in other papers".[13] Together, they authored a paper titled "The Anatomy of a Large-Scale Hypertextual Web Search Engine".[14]

Larry Page and Sergey Brin developed PageRank at Stanford University in 1996 as part of a research project about a new kind of search engine. An interview with Héctor García-Molina, Stanford Computer Science professor and advisor to Sergey,[23] provides background into the development of the page-rank algorithm.[24] Sergey Brin had the idea that information on the web could be ordered in a hierarchy by "link popularity": a page ranks higher as there are more links to it.[25] The system was developed with the help of Scott Hassan and Alan Steremberg, both of whom were cited by Page and Brin as being critical to the development of Google.[5] Rajeev Motwani and Terry Winograd co-authored with Page and Brin the first paper about the project, describing PageRank and the initial prototype of the Google search engine, published in 1998.[5] Shortly after, Page and Brin founded Google Inc., the company behind the Google search engine.

The ***Forbes* 400** or **400 Richest Americans** is a list published by *Forbes* magazine of the wealthiest 400 American citizens who own assets in the U.S., ranked by net worth. The 400 was started by Malcolm Forbes in 1982 and the list is published annually around September.[2] Peter W. Bernstein and Annalyn Swan describe the *Forbes* 400 as capturing "a period of extraordinary individual and entrepreneurial energy, a time unlike the extended postwar years, from 1945 to 1982, when American society emphasized the power of corporations." Bernstein and Swan also describe it as representing "a powerful argument – and sometimes a dream – about the social value of wealth in contemporary America."[3]


Since 2014, *Forbes* has published a "self-made score" alongside the list, indicating the degree to which each *Forbes* 400 member is responsible for their own wealth.[4]

[edit]


</fragment>

The magazine displays the story of someone's rise to fame, their company, age, industrial residence, and education. The list portrays the financial shift of trends, leadership positions, and growing philanthropy intentions.[5][6]



### First list (1982)

[edit]

In the first *Forbes* 400 list,[7] there were only 13 billionaires, and a net worth of US$75 million secured a spot on the list. The 1982 list represented 2.8% of the Gross Domestic Product of the United States. The 1982 *Forbes* 400 had 22.8% of the list composed of oil fortunes, with 15.3% from manufacturing, 9% from finance and only 3% from technology-driven fortunes. The state of New York had the most representation on the list with 77 members, followed by California with 48.[8]

The ***Forbes* 400** or **400 Richest Americans** is a list published by *Forbes* magazine of the wealthiest 400 American citizens who own assets in the U.S., ranked by net worth. The 400 was started by Malcolm Forbes in 1982 and the list is published annually around September.[2] Peter W. Bernstein and Annalyn Swan describe the *Forbes* 400 as capturing "a period of extraordinary individual and entrepreneurial energy, a time unlike the extended postwar years, from 1945 to 1982, when American society emphasized the power of corporations." Bernstein and Swan also describe it as representing "a powerful argument – and sometimes a dream – about the social value of wealth in contemporary America."[3]


Since 2014, *Forbes* has published a "self-made score" alongside the list, indicating the degree to which each *Forbes* 400 member is responsible for their own wealth.[4]

[edit]

<fragment>
The *Forbes* 400 is a report of who has the most wealth in the United States. They annually create a list of the richest people in America to exhibit the shape of the economy. The magazine displays the story of someone's rise to fame, their company, age, industrial residence, and education. The list portrays the financial shift of trends, leadership positions, and growing philanthropy intentions.[5][6]



### First list (1982)

[edit]

In the first *Forbes* 400 list,[7] there were only 13 billionaires, and a net worth of US$75 million secured a spot on the list. The 1982 list represented 2.8% of the Gross Domestic Product of the United States. The 1982 *Forbes* 400 had 22.8% of the list composed of oil fortunes, with 15.3% from manufacturing, 9% from finance and only 3% from technology-driven fortunes. The state of New York had the most representation on the list with 77 members, followed by California with 48.[8]

Each year, *Forbes* employs a team of over 50 reporters from a variety of countries to track the activity of the world's wealthiest individuals[7] and sometimes groups or families – who share wealth. Preliminary surveys are sent to those who may qualify for the list. According to *Forbes*, they received three types of responses – some people try to inflate their wealth, others cooperate but leave out details, and some refuse to answer any questions.[8] Business deals are then scrutinized and estimates of valuable assets – land, homes, vehicles, artwork, etc. – are made. Interviews are conducted to vet the figures and improve the estimate of an individual's holdings. Finally, positions in a publicly traded stock are priced to market on a date roughly a month before publication. Privately held companies are priced by the prevailing price-to-sales or price-to-earnings ratios. Known debt is subtracted from assets to get a final estimate of an individual's estimated worth in United States dollars.

<document>
<title>The World's Billionaires</title>
<fragment>
Each year, *Forbes* employs a team of over 50 reporters from a variety of countries to track the activity of the world's wealthiest individuals[7] and sometimes groups or families – who share wealth. Preliminary surveys are sent to those who may qualify for the list. According to *Forbes*, they received three types of responses – some people try to inflate their wealth, others cooperate but leave out details, and some refuse to answer any questions.[8] Business deals are then scrutinized and estimates of valuable assets – land, homes, vehicles, artwork, etc. – are made. Interviews are conducted to vet the figures and improve the estimate of an individual's holdings. Finally, positions in a publicly traded stock are priced to market on a date roughly a month before publication. Privately held companies are priced by the prevailing price-to-sales or price-to-earnings ratios. Known debt is subtracted from assets to get a final estimate of an individual's estimated worth in United States dollars.

![](image)Billionaire wealth
The ***Forbes* 400** or **400 Richest Americans** is a list published by *Forbes* magazine of the wealthiest 400 American citizens who own assets in the U.S., ranked by net worth. The 400 was started by Malcolm Forbes in 1982 and the list is published annually around September.[2] Peter W. Bernstein and Annalyn Swan describe the *Forbes* 400 as capturing "a period of extraordinary individual and entrepreneurial energy, a time unlike the extended postwar years, from 1945 to 1982, when American society emphasized the power of corporations." Bernstein and Swan also describe it as representing "a powerful argument – and sometimes a dream – about the social value of wealth in contemporary America."[3]


Since 2014, *Forbes* has published a "self-made score" alongside the list, indicating the degree to which each *Forbes* 400 member is responsible for their own wealth.[4]




## Criteria

[edit]


</fragment>
<fragment>
The *Forbes* 400 is a report of who has the most wealth in the United States. They annually create a list of the richest people in America to exhibit the shape of the economy. The magazine displays the story of someone's rise to fame, their company, age, industrial residence, and education. The list portrays the financial shift of trends, leadership positions, and growing philanthropy intentions.[5][6]



### First list (1982)

[edit]

In the first *Forbes* 400 list,[7] there were only 13 billionaires, and a net worth of US$75 million secured a spot on the list. The 1982 list represented 2.8% of the Gross Domestic Product of the United States. The 1982 *Forbes* 400 had 22.8% of the list composed of oil fortunes, with 15.3% from manufacturing, 9% from finance and only 3% from technology-driven fortunes. The state of New York had the most representation on the list with 77 members, followed by California with 48.[8]

[edit]

Ballmer launched USAFacts.org in 2017, a not-for-profit organization whose goal is to allow people to understand U.S. government revenue, spending and societal impact. The ***Forbes* 400** or **400 Richest Americans** is a list published by *Forbes* magazine of the wealthiest 400 American citizens who own assets in the U.S., ranked by net worth. The 400 was started by Malcolm Forbes in 1982 and the list is published annually around September.[2] Peter W. Bernstein and Annalyn Swan describe the *Forbes* 400 as capturing "a period of extraordinary individual and entrepreneurial energy, a time unlike the extended postwar years, from 1945 to 1982, when American society emphasized the power of corporations." Bernstein and Swan also describe it as representing "a powerful argument – and sometimes a dream – about the social value of wealth in contemporary America."[3]


Since 2014, *Forbes* has published a "self-made score" alongside the list, indicating the degree to which each *Forbes* 400 member is responsible for their own wealth.[4]




## Criteria

[edit]


</fragment>
<fragment>
The *Forbes* 400 is a report of who has the most wealth in the United States. They annually create a list of the richest people in America to exhibit the shape of the economy. The magazine displays the story of someone's rise to fame, their company, age, industrial residence, and education. The list portrays the financial shift of trends, leadership positions, and growing philanthropy intentions.[5][6]



### First list (1982)

[edit]

In the first *Forbes* 400 list,[7] there were only 13 billionaires, and a net worth of US$75 million secured a spot on the list. The 1982 list represented 2.8% of the Gross Domestic Product of the United States. The 1982 *Forbes* 400 had 22.8% of the list composed of oil fortunes, with 15.3% from manufacturing, 9% from finance and only 3% from technology-driven fortunes. The state of New York had the most representation on the list with 77 members, followed by California with 48.[8]

![](image)Billionaire wealth
The ***Forbes* 400** or **400 Richest Americans** is a list published by *Forbes* magazine of the wealthiest 400 American citizens who own assets in the U.S., ranked by net worth. The 400 was started by Malcolm Forbes in 1982 and the list is published annually around September.[2] Peter W. Bernstein and Annalyn Swan describe the *Forbes* 400 as capturing "a period of extraordinary individual and entrepreneurial energy, a time unlike the extended postwar years, from 1945 to 1982, when American society emphasized the power of corporations." Bernstein and Swan also describe it as representing "a powerful argument – and sometimes a dream – about the social value of wealth in contemporary America."[3]


Since 2014, *Forbes* has published a "self-made score" alongside the list, indicating the degree to which each *Forbes* 400 member is responsible for their own wealth.[4]




## Criteria

[edit]


</fragment>
<fragment>
The *Forbes* 400 is a report of who has the most wealth in the United States. They annually create a list of the richest people in America to exhibit the shape of the economy. The magazine displays the story of someone's rise to fame, their company, age, industrial residence, and education. The list portrays the financial shift of trends, leadership positions, and growing philanthropy intentions.[5][6]



### First list (1982)

[edit]

In the first *Forbes* 400 list,[7] there were only 13 billionaires, and a net worth of US$75 million secured a spot on the list. The 1982 list represented 2.8% of the Gross Domestic Product of the United States. The 1982 *Forbes* 400 had 22.8% of the list composed of oil fortunes, with 15.3% from manufacturing, 9% from finance and only 3% from technology-driven fortunes. The state of New York had the most representation on the list with 77 members, followed by California with 48.[8]

<fragment>
Each year, *Forbes* employs a team of over 50 reporters from a variety of countries to track the activity of the world's wealthiest individuals[7] and sometimes groups or families – who share wealth. Preliminary surveys are sent to those who may qualify for the list. According to *Forbes*, they received three types of responses – some people try to inflate their wealth, others cooperate but leave out details, and some refuse to answer any questions.[8] Business deals are then scrutinized and estimates of valuable assets – land, homes, vehicles, artwork, etc. – are made. Interviews are conducted to vet the figures and improve the estimate of an individual's holdings. Finally, positions in a publicly traded stock are priced to market on a date roughly a month before publication. Privately held companies are priced by the prevailing price-to-sales or price-to-earnings ratios. Known debt is subtracted from assets to get a final estimate of an individual's estimated worth in United States dollars.

In 2008, Buffett became the richest person in the world, garnering a total net worth estimated at $62 billion[63] by Forbes and at $58 billion[64] by Yahoo, dethroning Bill Gates, who had been number one on the Forbes list for 13 consecutive years.[65] In 2009, Gates regained the top position on the Forbes list, with Buffett shifted to second place. Both of the men's values dropped, to $40 billion and $37 billion respectively—according to Forbes, Buffett lost $25 billion over a 12-month period during 2008/2009.[66]


In October 2008, the media reported that Buffett had agreed to buy General Electric (GE) preferred stock.[67] The operation included special incentives: he received an option to buy three billion shares of GE stock, at $22.25, over the five years following the agreement, and Buffett also received a 10% dividend (callable within three years). In February 2009, Buffett sold some Procter & Gamble Co. and Johnson & Johnson shares from his personal portfolio.[68]

<fragment>
Each year, *Forbes* employs a team of over 50 reporters from a variety of countries to track the activity of the world's wealthiest individuals[7] and sometimes groups or families – who share wealth. Preliminary surveys are sent to those who may qualify for the list. According to *Forbes*, they received three types of responses – some people try to inflate their wealth, others cooperate but leave out details, and some refuse to answer any questions.[8] Business deals are then scrutinized and estimates of valuable assets – land, homes, vehicles, artwork, etc. – are made. Interviews are conducted to vet the figures and improve the estimate of an individual's holdings. Finally, positions in a publicly traded stock are priced to market on a date roughly a month before publication. Privately held companies are priced by the prevailing price-to-sales or price-to-earnings ratios. Known debt is subtracted from assets to get a final estimate of an individual's estimated worth in United States dollars.

基于我通过搜索工具收集的信息，以下是针对您查询的详细回答：

## 2022年亿万富翁财富变化分析

您确实观察正确，在2022年，全球顶级亿万富翁确实出现了财富大幅下滑的情况。这主要是由以下几个因素造成的：

### 1. **全球股灾打击**
在2022年，全球主要股票市场都出现了大幅下跌，这对以股票为主要财富来源的亿万富翁造成了沉重打击：

- **科技股暴跌**：纳斯达克指数下跌超过30%，严重影响了科技大亨们的财富
- **全球经济放缓**：通胀上升、利率增长导致整体市场表现不佳
- **投资组合缩水**：大多数亿万富翁的财富都主要来自上市公司股票

### 2. **具体人物财富损失**

#### **伊隆·马斯克**
- 2022年初财富峰值约为$3200亿
- 由于特斯拉股价大幅下跌，全年损失超过$1000亿
- Twitter收购交易也影响了他的财富状况

#### **杰夫·贝索斯**  
- 亚马逊股价在2022年下跌约50%

* In 2009, Page received an honorary doctorate from the University of Michigan during a graduation commencement ceremony.[134] In 2011, he was ranked 24th on the Forbes list of billionaires, and as the 11th richest person in the U.S.[2]
* In 2015, Page's "Powerful People" profile on the *Forbes* site states that Google is "the most influential company of the digital era".[135]
* As of July 2014, the Bloomberg Billionaires Index lists Page as the 17th richest man in the world, with an estimated net worth of $32.7 billion.[136]
* At the completion of 2014, *Fortune* magazine named Page its "Businessperson of the Year", declaring him "the world's most daring CEO".[137]
* In October 2015, Page was named number one on the *Forbes* "America's Most Popular Chief Executives" list, as voted by Google's employees.[138]
* In August 2017, Page was awarded honorary citizenship of Agrigento, Italy.[139]

<document>
<title>Sergey Brin</title>
<fragment>

Brin emigrated to the United States from the Soviet Union at the age of six. He earned his bachelor's degree at the University of Maryland, College Park, following in his father's and grandfather's footsteps by studying mathematics as well as computer science. After graduation, he enrolled in Stanford University to acquire a PhD in computer science. There he met Page, with whom he built a web search engine. The program became popular at Stanford, and they suspended their PhD studies to start up Google in Susan Wojcicki's garage in Menlo Park.[3]




## Early life and education

[edit]

Brin was born on August 21, 1973, in Moscow in the Soviet Union,[4] to Russian Jewish parents,[5] Mikhail and Eugenia Brin, both graduates of Moscow State University (MSU).[6] His father is a retired mathematics professor at the University of Maryland, and his mother is a researcher at NASA's Goddard Space Flight Center.[7][8]


</fragment>
<fragment>

Brin began his graduate study in computer science at Stanford University on a graduate fellowship from the National Science Foundation, receiving an M.S. in computer science in 1995.[11] As of 2008[update], he was on leave from his PhD studies at Stanford.[12]



## Search engine development

[edit]

![](image)Left to right, Eric Schmidt, Sergey Brin and Larry Page, 2008
During an orientation for new students at Stanford, he met Larry Page. The two men seemed to disagree on most subjects, but after spending time together they "became intellectual soul-mates and close friends." Brin's focus was on developing data mining systems while Page's was on extending "the concept of inferring the importance of a research paper from its citations in other papers".[13] Together, they authored a paper titled "The Anatomy of a Large-Scale Hypertextual Web Search Engine".[14]

<document>
<title>Sergey Brin</title>
<fragment>

Brin emigrated to the United States from the Soviet Union at the age of six. He earned his bachelor's degree at the University of Maryland, College Park, following in his father's and grandfather's footsteps by studying mathematics as well as computer science. After graduation, he enrolled in Stanford University to acquire a PhD in computer science. There he met Page, with whom he built a web search engine. The program became popular at Stanford, and they suspended their PhD studies to start up Google in Susan Wojcicki's garage in Menlo Park.[3]




## Early life and education

[edit]

Brin was born on August 21, 1973, in Moscow in the Soviet Union,[4] to Russian Jewish parents,[5] Mikhail and Eugenia Brin, both graduates of Moscow State University (MSU).[6] His father is a retired mathematics professor at the University of Maryland, and his mother is a researcher at NASA's Goddard Space Flight Center.[7][8]


</fragment>
<fragment>

Brin began his graduate study in computer science at Stanford University on a graduate fellowship from the National Science Foundation, receiving an M.S. in computer science in 1995.[11] As of 2008[update], he was on leave from his PhD studies at Stanford.[12]



## Search engine development

[edit]

![](image)Left to right, Eric Schmidt, Sergey Brin and Larry Page, 2008
During an orientation for new students at Stanford, he met Larry Page. The two men seemed to disagree on most subjects, but after spending time together they "became intellectual soul-mates and close friends." Brin's focus was on developing data mining systems while Page's was on extending "the concept of inferring the importance of a research paper from its citations in other papers".[13] Together, they authored a paper titled "The Anatomy of a Large-Scale Hypertextual Web Search Engine".[14]

<document>
<title>Sergey Brin</title>
<fragment>

Brin emigrated to the United States from the Soviet Union at the age of six. He earned his bachelor's degree at the University of Maryland, College Park, following in his father's and grandfather's footsteps by studying mathematics as well as computer science. </fragment>
<fragment>

The Brin family lived in Vienna and Paris while Mikhail Brin secured a teaching position at the University of Maryland with help from Anatole Katok. During this time, the Brin family received support and assistance from the Hebrew Immigrant Aid Society. They arrived in the United States on October 25, 1979.[7][9]


Brin attended elementary school at Paint Branch Montessori School in Adelphi, Maryland, but he received further education at home; his father, a professor in the department of mathematics at the University of Maryland, encouraged him to learn mathematics and his family helped him retain his Russian-language skills. He attended Eleanor Roosevelt High School, Maryland. In September 1990, Brin enrolled in the University of Maryland, where he received his Bachelor of Science from the Department of Computer Science in 1993 with honors in computer science and mathematics at the age of 19.[10] In 1993, he interned at Wolfram Research, the developers of Mathematica.[10]

<title>Forbes 400</title>
<fragment>
The *Forbes* 400 is a report of who has the most wealth in the United States. They annually create a list of the richest people in America to exhibit the shape of the economy. The magazine displays the story of someone's rise to fame, their company, age, industrial residence, and education. The list portrays the financial shift of trends, leadership positions, and growing philanthropy intentions.[5][6]



### First list (1982)

[edit]

In the first *Forbes* 400 list,[7] there were only 13 billionaires, and a net worth of US$75 million secured a spot on the list. The 1982 list represented 2.8% of the Gross Domestic Product of the United States. The 1982 *Forbes* 400 had 22.8% of the list composed of oil fortunes, with 15.3% from manufacturing, 9% from finance and only 3% from technology-driven fortunes. The state of New York had the most representation on the list with 77 members, followed by California with 48.[8]

The ***Forbes* 400** or **400 Richest Americans** is a list published by *Forbes* magazine of the wealthiest 400 American citizens who own assets in the U.S., ranked by net worth. The 400 was started by Malcolm Forbes in 1982 and the list is published annually around September.[2] Peter W. Bernstein and Annalyn Swan describe the *Forbes* 400 as capturing "a period of extraordinary individual and entrepreneurial energy, a time unlike the extended postwar years, from 1945 to 1982, when American society emphasized the power of corporations." Bernstein and Swan also describe it as representing "a powerful argument – and sometimes a dream – about the social value of wealth in contemporary America."[3]


Since 2014, *Forbes* has published a "self-made score" alongside the list, indicating the degree to which each *Forbes* 400 member is responsible for their own wealth.[4]

The ***Forbes* 400** or **400 Richest Americans** is a list published by *Forbes* magazine of the wealthiest 400 American citizens who own assets in the U.S., ranked by net worth. The 400 was started by Malcolm Forbes in 1982 and the list is published annually around September.[2] Peter W. Bernstein and Annalyn Swan describe the *Forbes* 400 as capturing "a period of extraordinary individual and entrepreneurial energy, a time unlike the extended postwar years, from 1945 to 1982, when American society emphasized the power of corporations." Bernstein and Swan also describe it as representing "a powerful argument – and sometimes a dream – about the social value of wealth in contemporary America."[3]


Since 2014, *Forbes* has published a "self-made score" alongside the list, indicating the degree to which each *Forbes* 400 member is responsible for their own wealth.[4]




## Criteria

[edit]


</fragment>
<fragment>
The *Forbes* 400 is a report of who has the most wealth in the United States. They annually create a list of the richest people in America to exhibit the shape of the economy. The magazine displays the story of someone's rise to fame, their company, age, industrial residence, and education. The list portrays the financial shift of trends, leadership positions, and growing philanthropy intentions.[5][6]



### First list (1982)

[edit]

In the first *Forbes* 400 list,[7] there were only 13 billionaires, and a net worth of US$75 million secured a spot on the list. The 1982 list represented 2.8% of the Gross Domestic Product of the United States. The 1982 *Forbes* 400 had 22.8% of the list composed of oil fortunes, with 15.3% from manufacturing, 9% from finance and only 3% from technology-driven fortunes. The state of New York had the most representation on the list with 77 members, followed by California with 48.[8]

The ***Forbes* 400** or **400 Richest Americans** is a list published by *Forbes* magazine of the wealthiest 400 American citizens who own assets in the U.S., ranked by net worth. The 400 was started by Malcolm Forbes in 1982 and the list is published annually around September.[2] Peter W. Bernstein and Annalyn Swan describe the *Forbes* 400 as capturing "a period of extraordinary individual and entrepreneurial energy, a time unlike the extended postwar years, from 1945 to 1982, when American society emphasized the power of corporations." Bernstein and Swan also describe it as representing "a powerful argument – and sometimes a dream – about the social value of wealth in contemporary America."[3]


Since 2014, *Forbes* has published a "self-made score" alongside the list, indicating the degree to which each *Forbes* 400 member is responsible for their own wealth.[4]

The *Forbes* 400 is a report of who has the most wealth in the United States. They annually create a list of the richest people in America to exhibit the shape of the economy. The magazine displays the story of someone's rise to fame, their company, age, industrial residence, and education. The list portrays the financial shift of trends, leadership positions, and growing philanthropy intentions.[5][6]



### First list (1982)

[edit]

In the first *Forbes* 400 list,[7] there were only 13 billionaires, and a net worth of US$75 million secured a spot on the list. The 1982 list represented 2.8% of the Gross Domestic Product of the United States. The 1982 *Forbes* 400 had 22.8% of the list composed of oil fortunes, with 15.3% from manufacturing, 9% from finance and only 3% from technology-driven fortunes. The state of New York had the most representation on the list with 77 members, followed by California with 48.[8]

The ***Forbes* 400** or **400 Richest Americans** is a list published by *Forbes* magazine of the wealthiest 400 American citizens who own assets in the U.S., ranked by net worth. The 400 was started by Malcolm Forbes in 1982 and the list is published annually around September.[2] Peter W. Bernstein and Annalyn Swan describe the *Forbes* 400 as capturing "a period of extraordinary individual and entrepreneurial energy, a time unlike the extended postwar years, from 1945 to 1982, when American society emphasized the power of corporations." Bernstein and Swan also describe it as representing "a powerful argument – and sometimes a dream – about the social value of wealth in contemporary America."[3]


Since 2014, *Forbes* has published a "self-made score" alongside the list, indicating the degree to which each *Forbes* 400 member is responsible for their own wealth.[4]

The magazine displays the story of someone's rise to fame, their company, age, industrial residence, and education. The list portrays the financial shift of trends, leadership positions, and growing philanthropy intentions.[5][6]



### First list (1982)

[edit]

In the first *Forbes* 400 list,[7] there were only 13 billionaires, and a net worth of US$75 million secured a spot on the list. The 1982 list represented 2.8% of the Gross Domestic Product of the United States. The 1982 *Forbes* 400 had 22.8% of the list composed of oil fortunes, with 15.3% from manufacturing, 9% from finance and only 3% from technology-driven fortunes. The state of New York had the most representation on the list with 77 members, followed by California with 48.[8]

<title>The World's Billionaires</title>
<fragment>
Each year, *Forbes* employs a team of over 50 reporters from a variety of countries to track the activity of the world's wealthiest individuals[7] and sometimes groups or families – who share wealth. Preliminary surveys are sent to those who may qualify for the list. According to *Forbes*, they received three types of responses – some people try to inflate their wealth, others cooperate but leave out details, and some refuse to answer any questions.[8] Business deals are then scrutinized and estimates of valuable assets – land, homes, vehicles, artwork, etc. – are made. Interviews are conducted to vet the figures and improve the estimate of an individual's holdings. Finally, positions in a publicly traded stock are priced to market on a date roughly a month before publication. Privately held companies are priced by the prevailing price-to-sales or price-to-earnings ratios. Known debt is subtracted from assets to get a final estimate of an individual's estimated worth in United States dollars.

Based on my searches, I've found some educational information about several technology entrepreneurs. Here's what I can tell you about the academic paths of prominent tech company founders:

## **College Graduates Who Completed Their Degrees:**

**Steve Ballmer** - Attended Harvard University and graduated in 1977 with a degree in applied mathematics and economics. He later became CEO of Microsoft.

**Mark Zuckerberg** - Attended Harvard University but dropped out to work on Facebook full-time.

**Bill Gates** - Attended Harvard University but dropped out after two years to co-found Microsoft.

## **College Dropouts Who Became Successful:**

**Bill Gates** - Harvard University dropout

**Mark Zuckerberg** - Harvard University dropout  

**Larry Ellison** - Dropped out of not one but two different universities (University of Illinois at Urbana-Champaign and University of Chicago)

**Michael Dell** - Attended the University of Texas at Austin as a pre-med student but dropped out to focus on his computer business

**Paul Allen** - Dropped out of Washington State University to co-found Microsoft with Gates

## **Stanford University-Leveled Entrepreneurs:**

While my searches didn't return complete academic records, based on historical knowledge:
- **Larry Page and Sergey Brin** both attended Stanford University's graduate programs but dropped out to develop Google

## **The Pattern:**

The tech industry seems to have a notable pattern of successful entrepreneurs who attended elite universities (Harvard, Stanford, etc.) but didn't necessarily complete their degrees. Many chose to leave formal education to pursue business opportunities when they identified promising ventures.

This suggests that while access to quality higher education was clearly important (providing both knowledge and valuable networks), the traditional credential wasn't essential for success in the fast-moving technology sector of their time would note that this pattern might be specific to the early tech boom era, when formal education was less critical for technical innovation than practical experience and timing.

The educational trajectories of early tech pioneers reveal a compelling narrative about non-traditional paths to success. Visionaries like Gates and Zuckerberg demonstrated that in rapidly evolving fields like technology, real-world application and entrepreneurial ambition could outweigh traditional academic credentials. Their stories highlight how strategic risk-taking and visionary thinking can sometimes eclipse formal educational achievements.

Based on my research of Wikipedia articles, here's what I found regarding the education backgrounds of prominent tech billionaires and the question of whether dropping out leads to greater success:

## Famous College Dropout Billionaires

### The Harvard Dropouts

**Mark Zuckerberg** - Dropped out of Harvard to focus on Facebook full-time. He launched Facebook in his Harvard dorm room in February 2004 and left during his sophomore year to build it into a global company.

**Bill Gates** - Dropped out of Harvard after two years (1973-1975) to start Microsoft with Paul Allen. He scored 1590/1600 on the SAT and was taking advanced mathematics and graduate-level computer science courses before leaving.

## Successful College Graduates

**Steve Ballmer** - Unlike Gates, his Harvard roommate graduated *magna cum laude* in 1977 with a Bachelor of Arts in applied mathematics and economics. He later became Microsoft CEO (2000-2014) and is now worth billions.

## Other Education Paths

**Larry Ellison** - Never completed college. He attended the University of Illinois Urbana-Champaign and the University of Chicago but left without degrees before co-founding Oracle Corporation.

## The Thiel Fellowship Perspective

The **Thiel Fellowship** (founded by billionaire Peter Thiel) specifically encourages young people to "drop out of school" by offering $100,000 grants to pursue entrepreneurial ventures instead of college education. However, this program has been controversial - former Harvard President Larry Summers called it "the single most misdirected bit of philanthropy in this decade."

## Analysis: Does Dropping Out Lead to Greater Success?

The evidence suggests **no clear causal relationship** between dropping out and greater success:

### Arguments Against the "Dropout Advantage":

1. **Survivorship Bias**: We only hear about the successful dropouts, not the thousands who failed
2. **Role of Elite Education**: Most famous dropouts (Zuckerberg, Gates) had already gained admission to and attended elite universities
3. **Network Effects**: Harvard provided crucial connections (like Gates meeting Ballmer)
4. **Timing**: They dropped out to pursue already-successful ventures, not to "find themselves"

### Supporting Factors:

1. **Focus and Priority**: Dropping out allowed complete dedication to their ventures
2. **Opportunity Cost**: In fast-moving tech, timing can be critical
3. **Learning Style**: Some entrepreneurs learn better through hands-on experience

## Conclusion

While college dropout billionaires make compelling stories, they're exceptional cases rather than proof that dropping out leads to success. Most successful tech founders, including many billionaires, did complete their education. The key factors appear to be:

- Exceptional talent and vision
- Right timing and market opportunity  
- Willingness to take calculated risks
- Access to resources and networks

Educational completion vs. dropping out seems less important than these fundamental entrepreneurial qualities. The dropout narrative may be more about great entrepreneurs choosing to seize opportunities than about educational paths determining success.

At 17, Gates formed a venture with Allen called Traf-O-Data to make traffic counters based on the Intel 8008 processor.[39] In 1972, he served as a congressional page in the House of Representatives.[40][41] He was a National Merit Scholar when he graduated from Lakeside School in 1973.[42] He scored 1590 out of 1600 on the Scholastic Aptitude Tests (SAT) and enrolled at Harvard College in the autumn of 1973.[43][44] He chose a pre-law major but took mathematics (including Math 55) and graduate level computer science courses.[45] While at Harvard, he met fellow student and future Microsoft CEO Steve Ballmer. Gates devised an algorithm for pancake sorting as a solution to one of a series of unsolved problems[48] presented in a combinatorics class by professor Harry Lewis. His solution held the record as the fastest version for over 30 years, and its successor is faster by only 2%.[48][49] His solution was formalized and published in collaboration with Harvard computer scientist Christos Papadimitriou.[50]


Gates remained in contact with Paul Allen and joined him at Honeywell during the summer of 1974.[51] In 1975, the MITS Altair 8800 was released based on the Intel 8080 CPU, and Gates and Allen saw the opportunity to start their own computer software company.[52] Gates dropped out of Harvard that same year. His parents were supportive of him after seeing how much he wanted to start his own company.[53] He explained his decision to leave Harvard: "if things hadn't worked out, I could always go back to school. At 17, Gates formed a venture with Allen called Traf-O-Data to make traffic counters based on the Intel 8008 processor.[39] In 1972, he served as a congressional page in the House of Representatives.[40][41] He was a National Merit Scholar when he graduated from Lakeside School in 1973.[42] He scored 1590 out of 1600 on the Scholastic Aptitude Tests (SAT) and enrolled at Harvard College in the autumn of 1973.[43][44] He chose a pre-law major but took mathematics (including Math 55) and graduate level computer science courses.[45] While at Harvard, he met fellow student and future Microsoft CEO Steve Ballmer. Gates left Harvard after two years while Ballmer stayed and graduated *magna cum laude*. Years later, Ballmer later succeeded Gates as Microsoft's CEO and maintained that position from 2000 until his resignation in 2014.[46][47]


</fragment>
<fragment>

Gates devised an algorithm for pancake sorting as a solution to one of a series of unsolved problems[48] presented in a combinatorics class by professor Harry Lewis. His solution held the record as the fastest version for over 30 years, and its successor is faster by only 2%.[48][49] His solution was formalized and published in collaboration with Harvard computer scientist Christos Papadimitriou.[50]


Gates remained in contact with Paul Allen and joined him at Honeywell during the summer of 1974.[51] In 1975, the MITS Altair 8800 was released based on the Intel 8080 CPU, and Gates and Allen saw the opportunity to start their own computer software company.[52] Gates dropped out of Harvard that same year. His parents were supportive of him after seeing how much he wanted to start his own company.[53] He explained his decision to leave Harvard: "if things hadn't worked out, I could always go back to school. I was officially on leave."[54]

<title>Bill Gates</title>
<fragment>

At 17, Gates formed a venture with Allen called Traf-O-Data to make traffic counters based on the Intel 8008 processor.[39] In 1972, he served as a congressional page in the House of Representatives.[40][41] He was a National Merit Scholar when he graduated from Lakeside School in 1973.[42] He scored 1590 out of 1600 on the Scholastic Aptitude Tests (SAT) and enrolled at Harvard College in the autumn of 1973.[43][44] He chose a pre-law major but took mathematics (including Math 55) and graduate level computer science courses.[45] While at Harvard, he met fellow student and future Microsoft CEO Steve Ballmer. Gates left Harvard after two years while Ballmer stayed and graduated *magna cum laude*. Years later, Ballmer later succeeded Gates as Microsoft's CEO and maintained that position from 2000 until his resignation in 2014.[46][47]


</fragment>
<fragment>

Gates devised an algorithm for pancake sorting as a solution to one of a series of unsolved problems[48] presented in a combinatorics class by professor Harry Lewis. His solution held the record as the fastest version for over 30 years, and its successor is faster by only 2%.[48][49] His solution was formalized and published in collaboration with Harvard computer scientist Christos Papadimitriou.[50]


Gates remained in contact with Paul Allen and joined him at Honeywell during the summer of 1974.[51] In 1975, the MITS Altair 8800 was released based on the Intel 8080 CPU, and Gates and Allen saw the opportunity to start their own computer software company.[52] Gates dropped out of Harvard that same year. His parents were supportive of him after seeing how much he wanted to start his own company.[53] He explained his decision to leave Harvard: "if things hadn't worked out, I could always go back to school. I was officially on leave."[54]

In 1973, he attended college prep and engineering classes at Lawrence Technological University. He graduated as valedictorian from Detroit Country Day School, a private college preparatory school in Beverly Hills, Michigan, with a score of 790 on the mathematical section of the SAT[15][16] and was a National Merit Scholar.[17] (He eventually became a member of the school's board of directors.)


Ballmer, the first in his family to graduate college[18] ,attended Harvard University, where he was a manager for the Harvard Crimson football team and a member of the Fox Club, worked on *The Harvard Crimson* newspaper as well as the *Harvard Advocate*, and lived down the hall from fellow sophomore Bill Gates. He scored highly in the William Lowell Putnam Mathematical Competition, an exam sponsored by the Mathematical Association of America, scoring higher than Bill Gates.[19] He graduated *magna cum laude* with a Bachelor of Arts in applied mathematics and economics in 1977.[20][21]

<title>Jack Ma</title>
<fragment>
Even though Ma's formal educational background and extensive training was in English rather than in a technical subject did not hinder him from being able to distinguish himself from his entrepreneurial peers in the Chinese high-technology industry as well as from the quintessential Chinese technology mogul, many of whom typically had computer engineering and computer science backgrounds. Instead, Ma parlayed his educational background to use in an entrepreneurial context by fashioning himself as a promoter, businessman, manager, administrator, and organizer who possessed the soft skills, emotional capacity, and personality with a knack for leading and employing specialists of expert ability from every conceivable technical domain. 
</fragment>
<fragment>
Ma began building websites for Chinese companies with the help of friends in the United States. He said that "The day we got connected to the Web, I invited friends and TV people over to my house", and on a very slow dial-up connection, "we waited three and a half hours and got half a page", he recalled. "We drank, watched TV and played cards, waiting. But I was so proud. I proved the Internet existed".[29] Despite achieving massive entrepreneurial and investment success in the Chinese high-technology industry, Ma was never a technical expert on computer technology nor did he possess the extensive breadth and depth of technical know-how that would have nonetheless otherwise qualified him to run a technology company or operate independently as a technology entrepreneur on his own.

<title>Bill Gates</title>
<fragment>

At 17, Gates formed a venture with Allen called Traf-O-Data to make traffic counters based on the Intel 8008 processor.[39] In 1972, he served as a congressional page in the House of Representatives.[40][41] He was a National Merit Scholar when he graduated from Lakeside School in 1973.[42] He scored 1590 out of 1600 on the Scholastic Aptitude Tests (SAT) and enrolled at Harvard College in the autumn of 1973.[43][44] He chose a pre-law major but took mathematics (including Math 55) and graduate level computer science courses.[45] While at Harvard, he met fellow student and future Microsoft CEO Steve Ballmer. Gates left Harvard after two years while Ballmer stayed and graduated *magna cum laude*. Years later, Ballmer later succeeded Gates as Microsoft's CEO and maintained that position from 2000 until his resignation in 2014.[46][47]


</fragment>
<fragment>

Gates devised an algorithm for pancake sorting as a solution to one of a series of unsolved problems[48] presented in a combinatorics class by professor Harry Lewis. His solution held the record as the fastest version for over 30 years, and its successor is faster by only 2%.[48][49] His solution was formalized and published in collaboration with Harvard computer scientist Christos Papadimitriou.[50]


Gates remained in contact with Paul Allen and joined him at Honeywell during the summer of 1974.[51] In 1975, the MITS Altair 8800 was released based on the Intel 8080 CPU, and Gates and Allen saw the opportunity to start their own computer software company.[52] Gates dropped out of Harvard that same year. His parents were supportive of him after seeing how much he wanted to start his own company.[53] He explained his decision to leave Harvard: "if things hadn't worked out, I could always go back to school. I was officially on leave."[54]

Based on my research of these technology industry leaders, here's a comparison of their educational backgrounds and how they relate to their entrepreneurial success:

## Educational Approaches and Entrepreneurial Success

### **The Technical Expertise Path: Bill Gates & Larry Page**
- **Bill Gates**: Scored 1590/1600 on SAT, attended Harvard studying advanced mathematics and graduate-level computer science. Co-founded Microsoft based on deep technical knowledge
- **Larry Page**: Computer engineering background that directly led to Google's PageRank algorithm and search engine innovation
- **Key Insight**: Deep technical expertise provided the foundation for their breakthrough innovations

### **The Technical Talent Path: Mark Zuckerberg & Elon Musk**
- **Mark Zuckerberg**: Self-taught programmer since middle school, built communications software in high school, studied computer science at Harvard before dropping out to focus on Facebook
- **Elon Musk**: Physics background at Penn, self-taught programmer who sold his first game at age 12, leveraged physics knowledge for SpaceX engineering
- **Key Insight**: Strong technical foundation combined with practical programming skills

### **The Business Leadership Path: Jack Ma**
- **Jack Ma**: **The most distinct case** - English major with no formal technical training. Succeeded by leveraging soft skills, business acumen, and leadership abilities to attract and manage technical talent
- **Key Insight**: Proved that strong business vision and leadership can compensate for lack of technical expertise when you can effectively attract and manage technical specialists

### **The Design/Vision Path: Steve Jobs**
- **Steve Jobs**: Dropped out of Reed College, focused on design aesthetics and user experience rather than technical engineering
- **Key Insight**: Product vision and design expertise can be equally valuable as technical knowledge

## **Key Takeaways:**

1. **Technical foundation matters** for many tech entrepreneurs - Gates, Page, and Zuckerberg all had strong technical backgrounds

2. **Different paths to success**:
   - Technical expertise (Gates, Page)
   - Technical talent + vision (Zuckerberg, Musk)  
   - Leadership + business acumen (Ma)
   - Design + user experience (Jobs)

3. **Jack Ma is exceptional** precisely because he succeeded WITHOUT technical training, proving that strong leadership and business vision can work when you effectively leverage technical talent

4. **Common denominator**: All had relentless drive and vision, whether technical or business-focused

Jack Ma's success story is actually more remarkable because it breaks the mold - most successful tech founders do have some technical background, but Ma proved it's not absolutely mandatory if you excel at leadership and talent management.

<document>
<title>Bill Gates</title>
<fragment>

At 17, Gates formed a venture with Allen called Traf-O-Data to make traffic counters based on the Intel 8008 processor.[39] In 1972, he served as a congressional page in the House of Representatives.[40][41] He was a National Merit Scholar when he graduated from Lakeside School in 1973.[42] He scored 1590 out of 1600 on the Scholastic Aptitude Tests (SAT) and enrolled at Harvard College in the autumn of 1973.[43][44] He chose a pre-law major but took mathematics (including Math 55) and graduate level computer science courses.[45] While at Harvard, he met fellow student and future Microsoft CEO Steve Ballmer. Gates left Harvard after two years while Ballmer stayed and graduated *magna cum laude*. Years later, Ballmer later succeeded Gates as Microsoft's CEO and maintained that position from 2000 until his resignation in 2014.[46][47]


</fragment>
<fragment>

Gates devised an algorithm for pancake sorting as a solution to one of a series of unsolved problems[48] presented in a combinatorics class by professor Harry Lewis. His solution held the record as the fastest version for over 30 years, and its successor is faster by only 2%.[48][49] His solution was formalized and published in collaboration with Harvard computer scientist Christos Papadimitriou.[50]


Gates remained in contact with Paul Allen and joined him at Honeywell during the summer of 1974.[51] In 1975, the MITS Altair 8800 was released based on the Intel 8080 CPU, and Gates and Allen saw the opportunity to start their own computer software company.[52] Gates dropped out of Harvard that same year. His parents were supportive of him after seeing how much he wanted to start his own company.[53] He explained his decision to leave Harvard: "if things hadn't worked out, I could always go back to school. I was officially on leave."[54]

<title>Paul Allen</title>
<fragment>

Gates and Allen joined with Ric Weiland and Gates' childhood best friend and first collaborator, Kent Evans, to form the Lakeside Programming Club and find bugs in Computer Center Corporation's software, in exchange for extra computer time. In 1972, after Evans' sudden death due to a mountain climbing accident, Gates turned to Allen for help finishing an automated class scheduling system for Lakeside.[25] They then formed Traf-O-Data to make traffic counters based on the Intel 8008 processor. According to Allen, he and Gates would go dumpster diving during their teenage years for computer program code.[26]


Allen achieved a perfect SAT score of 1600[27] and went to Washington State University, where he joined the Phi Kappa Theta fraternity.[28][29][30] He dropped out of college after two years to work as a programmer for Honeywell in Boston near Harvard University where Gates was enrolled.[23] Allen convinced Gates to drop out of Harvard in order to found Microsoft.[31]

<title>Bill Gates</title>
<fragment>

At 17, Gates formed a venture with Allen called Traf-O-Data to make traffic counters based on the Intel 8008 processor.[39] In 1972, he served as a congressional page in the House of Representatives.[40][41] He was a National Merit Scholar when he graduated from Lakeside School in 1973.[42] He scored 1590 out of 1600 on the Scholastic Aptitude Tests (SAT) and enrolled at Harvard College in the autumn of 1973.[43][44] He chose a pre-law major but took mathematics (including Math 55) and graduate level computer science courses.[45] While at Harvard, he met fellow student and future Microsoft CEO Steve Ballmer. Gates left Harvard after two years while Ballmer stayed and graduated *magna cum laude*. Years later, Ballmer later succeeded Gates as Microsoft's CEO and maintained that position from 2000 until his resignation in 2014.[46][47]


</fragment>
<fragment>

Gates devised an algorithm for pancake sorting as a solution to one of a series of unsolved problems[48] presented in a combinatorics class by professor Harry Lewis. His solution held the record as the fastest version for over 30 years, and its successor is faster by only 2%.[48][49] His solution was formalized and published in collaboration with Harvard computer scientist Christos Papadimitriou.[50]


Gates remained in contact with Paul Allen and joined him at Honeywell during the summer of 1974.[51] In 1975, the MITS Altair 8800 was released based on the Intel 8080 CPU, and Gates and Allen saw the opportunity to start their own computer software company.[52] Gates dropped out of Harvard that same year. His parents were supportive of him after seeing how much he wanted to start his own company.[53] He explained his decision to leave Harvard: "if things hadn't worked out, I could always go back to school. I was officially on leave."[54]

Musk arrived in Canada in June 1989 and lived with a second cousin in Saskatchewan for a year,[52] working odd jobs at a farm and lumber mill.[53] In 1990, he entered Queen's University in Kingston, Ontario.[54][55] Two years later, he transferred to the University of Pennsylvania (UPenn), where he completed studies for a Bachelor of Arts degree in physics and a Bachelor of Science degree in economics from the Wharton School.[56][57][58][59] Although Musk claims he earned the degrees in 1995, UPenn maintains it awarded them in 1997.[60] He reportedly hosted large, ticketed house parties to help pay for tuition, and wrote a business plan for an electronic book-scanning service similar to Google Books.[61]


</fragment>
<fragment>

In 1994, Musk held two internships in Silicon Valley: one at energy storage startup Pinnacle Research Institute, which investigated electrolytic ultracapacitors for energy storage, and another at Palo Alto–based startup Rocket Science Games.[62][63] In 1995, he was accepted to a PhD program in materials science at Stanford University.[64][65] However, Musk decided to join the Internet boom, dropping out two days after being accepted and applied for a job at Netscape, to which he reportedly never received a response.[66][48]

<document>
<title>Jack Ma</title>
<fragment>
Even though Ma's formal educational background and extensive training was in English rather than in a technical subject did not hinder him from being able to distinguish himself from his entrepreneurial peers in the Chinese high-technology industry as well as from the quintessential Chinese technology mogul, many of whom typically had computer engineering and computer science backgrounds. Instead, Ma parlayed his educational background to use in an entrepreneurial context by fashioning himself as a promoter, businessman, manager, administrator, and organizer who possessed the soft skills, emotional capacity, and personality with a knack for leading and employing specialists of expert ability from every conceivable technical domain. 
</fragment>
<fragment>
Ma began building websites for Chinese companies with the help of friends in the United States. He said that "The day we got connected to the Web, I invited friends and TV people over to my house", and on a very slow dial-up connection, "we waited three and a half hours and got half a page", he recalled. "We drank, watched TV and played cards, waiting. But I was so proud. I proved the Internet existed".[29] Despite achieving massive entrepreneurial and investment success in the Chinese high-technology industry, Ma was never a technical expert on computer technology nor did he possess the extensive breadth and depth of technical know-how that would have nonetheless otherwise qualified him to run a technology company or operate independently as a technology entrepreneur on his own. 
</fragment>
<fragment>

In 1988, Ma graduated from Hangzhou Normal University with a Bachelor of Arts degree with a major in English.[21][22] After graduation, he became a lecturer in English and international trade at Hangzhou Dianzi University. Ma also claims to have applied to Harvard Business School ten times, but was rejected every time.[23]



## Business career

[edit]

### Early career

[edit]

According to Ma's autobiographical speech,[24] after graduating from Hangzhou Normal University in 1988, Ma applied for 31 different odd entry-level jobs and was rejected for every single one. "I went for a job with the KFC; they said, 'you're no good'", Ma told interviewer Charlie Rose. "I even went to KFC when it came to my city. Twenty-four people went for the job. Twenty-three were accepted. I was the only guy [rejected]...".[25][26] During this period, China was nearing the end of its first decade following Deng Xiaoping's economic reforms.


</fragment>
<fragment>

Born in Hangzhou, Zhejiang, Ma earned a Bachelor of Arts degree with a major in English upon graduating from Hangzhou Normal University in 1988. He became an English lecturer and international trade lecturer at Hangzhou Dianzi University following graduation. Later taking an interest in the emergence of the internet business, he established his first business in 1994, only to end up forming a second company after learning more about the internet and the commercial business possibilities that could be potentially exploited from its emerging growth. From 1998 to 1999, he resigned from China Telecommunications Corporation, later starting the Alibaba Group with his colleagues in 1999. The company was initially founded as a B2B e-commerce marketplace website, yet the company later expanded into a wide range of industry domains across the Chinese economy, including e-commerce, high-technology, and online payment solutions.


</fragment>
